summary:
Uruguay's trans-protection framework is statutory and national. The Comprehensive Law for Trans People (Law No. 19684) was promulgated by the Executive on 26 October 2018 and guarantees identity, health and anti-discrimination rights, obliges authorities to treat trans people respectfully, and bars denial of health services. It builds on Law No. 18.620 of 2009, which establishes the right to free development of personality in accordance with self-perceived gender identity, independent of biological, genetic, anatomical, morphological, hormonal or assigned sex.

Legal gender recognition is administrative and rests on self-declaration. Since October 2018 no surgery, hormone therapy or diagnosis is required to change legal gender on official documents. Adults have been able to change name and legal gender since October 2009; minors may do so with parental consent under the 2018 law. Under Law No. 18.620 the route runs through a voluntary Family Court process with a specialised multidisciplinary report, requiring proof of discordance with the registered name or sex and that the identity has been stable and persistent for at least two years; changes are notified to civil-identification and electoral authorities, and the person retains the same identity, passport and civic-credential number while exercising the rights attached to the new sex condition.

Official documents carry only female and male markers. Article 4c of Law No. 19684 recognises non-binary people in its definitions, but no third marker exists; a 2022 survey of non-binary people cites the absence of such a marker as deterring use of the legal change procedure.

Hate-crime and anti-discrimination machinery covers sexual orientation and sexual identity. Incitement to hatred on those grounds has been prohibited since 2003, and Penal Code article 149ter provides enhanced penalties for crimes motivated by them. The 2004 anti-discrimination law created an Honorary Commission to Combat Racial Discrimination, Xenophobia and other forms of Discrimination, with a mandate covering sexual orientation and sexual identity. The 2017 Mental Health Law (Law No. 19529) bars any mental-health diagnosis made on the exclusive basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. Article 22 of Law No. 19580, in force since January 2018, prohibits unnecessary medical procedures on intersex children and teenagers; intersex bodily-autonomy protections remain incomplete.

Partner recognition is settled. Civil unions have been available since 1 January 2008 under a law signed on 27 December 2007, requiring at least five years of cohabitation and granting health, inheritance, parenting and pension rights. Marriage has been open to same-sex couples since August 2013, and joint adoption by same-sex couples in a civil union has been permitted since September 2009, the first such provision in Latin America. The 2013 marriage law allows lesbian couples access to in vitro fertilisation, and on 3 October 2018 a family judge ruled that barring an unmarried lesbian couple from giving twins both surnames constituted sexual orientation discrimination.

Open service in the military has been permitted since May 2009 under a Defence Minister decree ending orientation discrimination in recruitment. Since 16 December 2020 gay and bisexual men donate blood under the same conditions as the rest of the population, ending the previous 12-month abstinence requirement. The age of consent has been equal at 15 regardless of orientation or gender since 1934.

Violence against trans residents is documented and, in at least one case, prosecuted. Joana, a 29-year-old trans woman, was shot dead in her Montevideo home on 28 July 2025; a suspect was subsequently sentenced to seven years for the murder. Survey data cited in country coverage records that about two-thirds of transgender Uruguayans report having been victims of physical violence, and state health service figures put transgender life expectancy at about 45 years against a national average of 77.

Enforcement against discrimination is uneven. In May 2024 a trans health-service user, Andreina Stuart, denounced mistreatment and discrimination at San Carlos hospital in Maldonado; a criminal complaint is pending and the hospital director pledged an administrative investigation once the judicial stage concludes, with local officials pressing for health-system updates. In a separate case, Beccah Rivas, a trans woman, sued the state bank BROU over discriminatory handling by a Prosegur guard and alleges the bank withheld the key camera footage; prosecutor Tania Vidal compelled the bank to produce material, and Rivas says she was dismissed after publicising the case.

In custody, national authorities have stated that a trans person entering the prison system has the right to decide whether to be placed in a men's or women's prison, and trans women are currently held in female prisons. A new prison planned for Montevideo is to include a specific sector for the trans population, and the new women's prison at Punta de Rieles would for the first time account for trans inmates. The Parliamentary Commissioner for the prison system, Juan Miguel Petit, described the sector as good news for a very vulnerable population and estimated it would be ready in under two years; National Rehabilitation Institute director Luis Mendoza told a parliamentary hearing that the laws are advanced but the mentality and infrastructure are not in line. Official figures record 14,965 people deprived of liberty, including 28 trans women and nine trans men.

Political opposition to the 2018 law exists but has not prevailed. A pre-referendum to repeal it went to the polls on 4 August 2019 and failed, with turnout of about 10 percent against the 25 percent of the electoral roll, roughly 650,000 voters, required to trigger a repeal consultation; the law remains in force. The Archbishop of Montevideo had called same-sex adoption a serious error, and about 69,360 signatures were gathered between November 2018 and March 2019 for the pre-referendum. Freedom House rated Uruguay Free in 2024 at 96/100, with political rights at 40/40 and civil liberties at 56/60. A 2014 poll found about 71 percent of Uruguayans supported same-sex marriage, the highest in South America, and Montevideo Pride has run annually since the 1990s, drawing an estimated 120,000 people in 2018, with Punta Pride held in Punta del Este each February.

Same-sex relations are legal nationwide, legal gender recognition is available, and LGBTI organisations can register. Equaldex records that in Montevideo, where national law applies, marriage, legal gender change, non-discrimination protections, the conversion-therapy ban and an equal age of consent are all in force, and hate-crime rules cover sexual orientation and gender identity.
tangentialFactors:
Regional comparisons place Uruguay at the top of Latin American rankings on LGBT inclusion. A 2015 Gay Happiness Index ranked it fifth with a score of 73, on a par with Canada and the Nordic countries, and in 2016 Americas Quarterly named it the most LGBT-friendly country in Latin America, calling it a model for social inclusion. Uruguay hosted the region's first international LGBT rights conference in July 2016, with hundreds of diplomats, politicians and activists attending.

Commercial and social infrastructure is concentrated in Montevideo, which has several gay bars, restaurants and pubs and is frequently described as one of the most gay-friendly cities in the region; Punta del Este hosts Punta Pride each February. These indices describe general social climate rather than conditions specific to trans residents, whose documented outcomes in health, education and employment diverge sharply from the country's overall standing.
localsOnly:
Youth and adult outcomes for trans residents are severe. Twenty-five percent of transgender Uruguayans left home before the age of 18 after family rejection, 87 percent did not finish secondary school, and other studies record about 75 percent expelled from the education system. Only 23 percent hold formal employment, and 67 percent report engaging in prostitution for income. The 2018 law mandates that transgender people receive 1 percent of public and private educational scholarships, calls on government to include them in housing programmes, and provides monetary reparations to transgender people persecuted during the Uruguayan dictatorship, estimated at around 50 people. In July 2019 the state water company Obras Sanitarias del Estado began offering jobs to transgender people in compliance with the law.

Country coverage estimates the transgender population at about 1,000 people. The dictatorship era involved torture, sexual violence and unjustified imprisonment of trans people.
outOfScopeNotes: Several items remain unresolved. The criminal complaint over the alleged mistreatment of Andreina Stuart at San Carlos hospital was pending, with the hospital's administrative investigation deferred until the judicial stage concludes. The outcome of Beccah Rivas's suit against the state bank BROU is not recorded in the sources consulted. The trans sector in the planned Montevideo prison was estimated in July 2023 to be ready in under two years; no source confirms whether it has opened. Intersex bodily-autonomy protections are described as incomplete, and no third gender marker has been introduced despite article 4c of Law No. 19684 recognising non-binary people in its definitions.
